scams.name: San Antonio Riverwalk Restaurant Overcharge & 'Scenic' Menu Markup
scams.description:
The River Walk is San Antonio's signature tourist attraction, but the riverside restaurants run significant tourist markups. The common patterns are these: (1) menu prices 30–60% above comparable non-tourist San Antonio restaurants (a $16 fajita plate at Mi Tierra becomes $28 at river-level venues); (2) an 18–22% auto-gratuity added to parties of two to four without clear menu disclosure; (3) a "river view" or "patio fee" of $3–$8 per person; (4) well drinks at $14–$17 (a standard San Antonio bar charges $8–$11); and (5) "scenic cruise" upsells at $30–$40 when direct San Antonio River Cruise tickets are $15–$17.

Travelers widely agree on the River Walk's overpricing, describing it as an overrated tourist draw and a gentrified tourist strip. For older travelers enjoying the River Walk, the practical playbook is straightforward: (1) book the San Antonio River Cruise (riosanantonio.com, $15 per adult, a 35-minute narrated boat tour) directly — not "Riverwalk VIP Cruise" packages at $40 and up; (2) for authentic Tex-Mex at fair prices, walk 10 minutes to Mi Tierra Café (open 24/7 at Market Square, $14–$22) or La Gloria ($16–$24) rather than riverside Casa Rio or Boudro's at $28–$40; (3) ALWAYS check the bill for auto-gratuity, a "river view fee," and service charges BEFORE tipping; (4) for margaritas at fair prices, walk to The Esquire Tavern (the oldest bar in Texas, $10–$14) one block north; and (5) the River Walk itself is FREE to walk — no "access fee" exists, despite occasional tout claims.
scams.avoidance: Book the River Cruise directly at riosanantonio.com ($15, 35-minute narrated tour). Walk 10 minutes to Market Square for Mi Tierra (open 24/7) or La Gloria at fair prices. Check the bill for auto-gratuity and a "river view fee" BEFORE tipping. For margaritas at fair prices, walk to The Esquire Tavern (the oldest bar in Texas). The River Walk path is FREE — no "access fee" exists.
scams.location: San Antonio River Walk, Paseo del Rio restaurants, Commerce Street bridge dining, Rivercenter Mall dining deck
scams.tldr: Riverside River Walk restaurants charge 30–60% above in-town prices, add undisclosed auto-gratuity and "river view" fees, and upsell $40 cruise packages.

scams.name: SAT Airport Rideshare, Taxi & 'Airport Parking' Tow Scam
scams.description:
SAT is 8 miles from downtown San Antonio, and legitimate fares are these: Uber or Lyft, $18–$28; a licensed taxi with a meter, $28–$35; and VIA Metropolitan Transit Route 5 Airport Express, $1.30 (scam-proof). Travelers warn about the off-airport "airport parking" tow lot: third-party websites advertise "SAT long-term parking, $8/day" at unlicensed lots that tow the car after 24 hours, claim "expired parking fees," and demand $300–$800 cash to release it. Other variants include (1) drivers at baggage claim offering a "flat $50" downtown (the legitimate fare is $18–$28); (2) "limo" touts quoting $100 and up for standard trips; (3) a driver demanding a cash tip beyond the app total; and (4) Uber surge pricing at $55 and up when a licensed taxi is $28–$35.

For older travelers arriving at SAT, the clean playbook is this: (1) take Uber or Lyft at the designated pickup zone with a fare screenshot ($18–$28 to downtown); (2) take a licensed taxi at the official taxi queue with the meter running, $28–$35 to downtown; (3) take VIA Route 5 Airport Express for $1.30 — the cheapest option, running 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; (4) for airport parking, use ONLY on-airport SAT lots (Economy $12/day, Long-Term $15/day, Garage $21/day) via sanantonioparking.com — NEVER off-airport sites advertising under $10/day; (5) refuse drivers soliciting at baggage claim; and (6) compare Uber surge pricing against the taxi-stand price at peak times.
scams.avoidance: Take Uber or Lyft at the designated pickup with a fare screenshot ($18–$28). Take a licensed taxi at the official queue with a meter: $28–$35 to downtown. VIA Route 5 Airport Express is $1.30 (6 a.m.–10 p.m.). For airport parking, use ONLY on-airport SAT lots via sanantonioparking.com. Refuse drivers soliciting at baggage claim.
scams.location: San Antonio International Airport (SAT) Terminal A/B baggage claim, off-airport parking lots, rideshare pickup zone
scams.tldr: Off-airport "$8/day" parking lots tow your car after 24 hours and demand $300–$800 cash; baggage-claim drivers and surge pricing inflate the 8-mile downtown trip.

scams.name: San Antonio Rental Car 'Damage Claim' & Alamo Upsell Scam
scams.description:
San Antonio is a major rental-car market serving River Walk visitors, Texas Hill Country day-trippers, and Austin/Houston route rentals, and travelers report a $3,000 Alamo Rent-A-Car damage claim that fits the pattern exactly. The scam variants at SAT and downtown include (1) counter-agent pressure to accept "zero-excess" insurance at two to three times what credit-card coverage provides; (2) a post-return "damage claim" of $2,000–$3,000 and up for pre-existing or fabricated scratches, often weeks after the return; (3) a fuel-policy "return full" claim where the alleged level is 0.1 gallon less than the documented fill; and (4) a toll-system "convenience fee" of $15 and up per toll, plus the toll itself.

Alamo, Hertz, and Budget at SAT have been named in multiple 2024–2025 damage-claim complaints. For older travelers renting at SAT, the protective playbook is this: (1) at pickup, take a video walk-around narrating EVERY visible scratch, tire condition, and wheel; (2) photograph all four sides, the roof, the wheels, and the undercarriage with your phone camera and a timestamp; (3) decline "zero-excess" insurance if your credit card provides rental coverage (Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum, and most Visa Signature cards do); (4) for TxTag tolls on the Austin route, pre-arrange a pass at the counter or pay cash at the plazas — NEVER use an "automatic toll plan" with a $15-per-toll "admin fee"; (5) return the car with the same fuel level documented at pickup; (6) dispute any post-return damage claim with your credit card within 48 hours using photo and video evidence; and (7) avoid Budget and Thrifty at SAT, which have the highest damage-claim complaint rates — use Enterprise or Avis instead.
scams.avoidance: Take a video walk-around at pickup narrating every scratch, tire, and wheel. Photograph all four sides, the roof, the wheels, and the undercarriage with a timestamp. Decline zero-excess insurance if your credit card provides rental coverage. Pre-arrange a TxTag or pay cash — skip the "automatic toll plan." Dispute any post-return damage with your credit card within 48 hours using photo and video evidence.
scams.location: SAT airport rental car facility (Terminal A/B adjacent), Enterprise/Alamo/Hertz San Antonio downtown offices
scams.tldr: Rental agents push overpriced "zero-excess" insurance and file $2,000–$3,000 damage claims weeks later for pre-existing or fabricated scratches.

scams.name: Alamo Mission 'Ticket' & Historic Site Tour Confusion
scams.description:
The Alamo Mission is FREE to enter — the Texas General Land Office operates it, and admission is $0 per person (thealamo.org). Timed-entry tickets for the church building are required at peak times and are free via advance booking at thealamo.org. The scam variants target tourists who are unaware of the free entry: (1) third-party websites selling "Alamo Skip-the-Line Tickets" at $25–$45 (there is no skip-the-line; free timed entry handles peak demand); (2) curb touts near the Alamo offering a "$40 Alamo + River Walk combo tour" when both are free to access; (3) "professional photographer" touts charging $15–$25 for unsolicited Alamo photos; (4) "Alamo Guided Audio Tour" upsells at $25 and up when the free timed-entry admission includes ranger-led talks; and (5) "Alamo Museum ticket" scams — the adjacent Alamo Cenotaph area is free, and the only legitimate paid Alamo experience is the movie "The Alamo: The Price of Freedom" at $20.

For older travelers visiting the Alamo, the clean playbook is this: (1) book free timed-entry tickets at thealamo.org one to seven days ahead during peak season (March–May, October–December); (2) REFUSE any third-party "Alamo skip-the-line" reseller — they're selling air; (3) Alamo Plaza, outside, is always free to walk, and the church interior is free with timed entry; (4) the official theater experience "The Alamo: The Price of Freedom" at $20 is the only legitimate paid Alamo upsell; (5) refuse unsolicited "photographer" approaches and take your own photos; and (6) Texas General Land Office rangers offer free 15-minute historical talks throughout the day — no tour guide needed. The Alamo can feel smaller than visitors expect.
scams.avoidance: Book free timed-entry tickets at thealamo.org one to seven days ahead. Refuse ALL third-party "Alamo skip-the-line" resellers — they're fake. Free ranger-led talks run throughout the day at the Alamo Mission. The only legitimate paid experience is the movie "The Alamo: The Price of Freedom" ($20). Take your own photos and refuse unsolicited "photographer" approaches.
scams.location: Alamo Plaza, Alamo Mission entrance queue, Crockett Street sightseeing-tour kiosks, Houston Street Alamo-adjacent venues
scams.tldr: The Alamo is free to enter, but third-party sites sell fake "skip-the-line" tickets and touts hawk $40 "combo tours" bundling two free attractions.

scams.name: Texas Hill Country 'Texas Winos' Wine Tour Scam
scams.description:
Travelers report a specific Texas Hill Country wine-tour operator, Texas Winos LLC, that took customer bookings via Groupon, Facebook, and third-party sites and charged $99–$149 per person for "all-inclusive" Fredericksburg wine tours, then failed to show up, canceled on arrival, or delivered a two-hour bus ride with 20-minute tastings at two wineries rather than the advertised five or six. Similar shell operators include "Texas Hill Country Wine Express," "Lone Star Wine Tours," and "Austin Wine Country Shuttle." Legitimate operators include Texas Wine Tours (texaswinetours.com, $149 per person, six wineries), Fredericksburg Wine Shuttle ($39, shuttle only), and the Grape Creek Vineyard shuttle (free to tasting-room customers).

For older travelers wanting a Texas Hill Country wine day from San Antonio, the clean playbook is this: (1) book ONLY with established operators — Texas Wine Tours (texaswinetours.com), Fredericksburg Wine Shuttle (fbgwineshuttle.com), or directly with individual wineries like Becker Vineyards, William Chris, Grape Creek, Messina Hof, or 4.0 Cellars; (2) verify the operator's BBB rating and look for 50 or more Google reviews at 4.5 stars or higher before paying; (3) REFUSE Groupon, Facebook Marketplace, or off-platform "wine tour" deals — the "Texas Winos" pattern — and pay by credit card (not Zelle or Venmo) for chargeback leverage; (4) book two to four weeks ahead for weekends (Fredericksburg peaks in March–May and October); (5) self-driving is an option (San Antonio to Fredericksburg is 70 miles, about 1.5 hours) but requires a designated driver; and (6) the Hill Country has more than 40 wineries, so quality over quantity matters more than "all-inclusive six-winery" promises.
scams.avoidance: Book Texas Wine Tours (texaswinetours.com) or Fredericksburg Wine Shuttle (fbgwineshuttle.com). Verify the BBB rating and look for 50 or more Google reviews at 4.5 stars or higher. Refuse Groupon, Facebook, or off-platform "wine tour" deals. Pay by credit card for chargeback leverage. Book two to four weeks ahead for weekends in the peak spring and fall seasons.
scams.location: Fredericksburg TX wine-tour operators, San Antonio hotel-concierge wine-tour desks, Texas Hill Country 290 Wine Road, Highway 290 winery strip
scams.tldr: A Hill Country tour operator takes $99–$149 Groupon bookings for "all-inclusive" Fredericksburg wine tours, then no-shows, cancels on arrival, or delivers far less than advertised.

scams.name: San Antonio STR 'Alamo Homes' & Fiesta-Season Airbnb Booking Fraud
scams.description:
Travelers warn against doing business with the "Alamo Homes" short-term-rental operator, citing off-platform bookings, deposits not returned, and double-bookings. During Fiesta San Antonio (10 days in late April each year), along with the King William Fair, the Battle of Flowers Parade, and NIOSA (Night in Old San Antonio), short-term-rental demand spikes and scams multiply. The scam variants include (1) off-platform "Airbnb" listings asking for a Zelle, Venmo, or wire transfer at a "15% discount" — the listing is fake and the money disappears; (2) cloned listings copying legitimate Airbnb photos onto Craigslist or Facebook Marketplace; (3) Fiesta-weekend "last-minute" rentals advertised on social media with Zelle-only payment; (4) "Alamo Homes" or similar-brand operators demanding off-platform booking; and (5) "wristband" resale scams in which fake "VIP wristbands" for NIOSA or the Battle of Flowers are sold at three to five times the legitimate $22–$38 prices.

For older travelers booking San Antonio accommodation, especially during Fiesta season, the protective playbook is this: (1) book ONLY through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment — NEVER Zelle, Venmo, Cash App, or wire transfer; (2) verify operator reviews (50 or more at 4.5 stars or higher) before paying; (3) for Fiesta in late April, book six to nine months ahead; (4) for Fiesta wristbands and event tickets, buy ONLY at fiesta-sa.org or at official event gates — NOT from social-media resellers or Facebook Marketplace; (5) legitimate San Antonio hotels include the Hyatt Regency River Walk, Marriott Rivercenter, La Cantera Resort, the Menger Hotel (historic, next to the Alamo), and Hotel Havana; and (6) report short-term-rental fraud to San Antonio Development Services (sanantonio.gov/DSD) and to the BBB.
scams.avoidance: Book ONLY through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com platform payment. NEVER pay via Zelle, Venmo, Cash App, or wire transfer. For Fiesta in late April, book six to nine months ahead. Buy Fiesta wristbands at fiesta-sa.org or official gates only. Legitimate hotels include the Hyatt River Walk, Marriott Rivercenter, La Cantera, and the Menger.
scams.location: Downtown San Antonio STRs, King William Historic District vacation rentals, Pearl District short-term rentals, Fiesta event-zone rentals
scams.tldr: Off-platform "Airbnb" listings and brands like "Alamo Homes" demand Zelle or wire payment for fake or double-booked rentals, with scams spiking during Fiesta in late April.
